turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello, doctor. Yes, nice to meet you too. I really appreciate you taking the time to see me. You know, it’s a bit funny me being here, because usually people my age are at the doctor for their joints or their blood pressure, but... well, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m constantly on the go. 

I’m always puttering around the house, fixing things that honestly probably don't even need fixing, or arranging things. Just the other day I took every single thing out of the front hall closet to wipe it down and rearrange all the winter coats and umbrellas by color, which took hours, but I just had to be doing something. And it's not just at home, either. I'm always volunteering for one more thing at the church or the library. Someone will ask for help with a bake sale or organizing a charity drive, and my hand shoots right up to take it on before I've even thought it through. 

It’s just... well, I’m 87 years old! You would think at my age I’d be ready to put my feet up and relax like everyone else I know. My friends are perfectly happy sitting in their recliners, but I have such a hard time just sitting down and being still. I try to sit in the living room and read the paper, and five minutes later I'm up again because I remembered the plants need watering or a picture frame looks crooked. It's just constant, and I don't know why I can't just rest.

turns.doctor_question: Do you get unwanted thoughts that keep bothering you until you do something a certain way?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, heavens no, it’s nothing like that. I know exactly what you mean, though—like my sister-in-law, Betty, rest her soul. She used to have to check the stove knobs three or four times before we could even leave the house for Sunday service, or she’d just be worried sick the whole time the pastor was speaking. But no, I don't get any of those... what did you call them? Unwanted thoughts. 

It’s not that I feel forced to do things a certain way because a thought is bothering me or scaring me. If I arrange that front hall closet by color, it’s not because a thought made me do it or because I'm worried something bad will happen if the red coats touch the blue ones. It’s just because I was standing there and thought, "Oh, wouldn't this be a nice little project?" and then I just dive right in before I can stop myself. 

My mind doesn't really get stuck on one thing bothering me, it's more like it just... well, it just bounces around to the next thing I could be doing. Like, I'll be in the kitchen and see a spot on the floor, and I'll wipe it, but I don't *have* to do it a specific way. I just do it because I have the energy and I can't seem to just walk past it and go sit down in my chair. I just always have to be busy, but it's never because my thoughts are nagging at me to do it perfectly, if that makes sense. So, no, no thoughts bothering me like that at all.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes having constant energy, being unable to just sit down, and always needing to be busy.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been needing less sleep than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, no, no, not at all. I sleep just as much as I always have, thank goodness. You know, you hear about people getting older and suddenly they only sleep four hours a night and wake up at the crack of dawn to just stare at the ceiling—like my neighbor, Martha, she tells me she’s up at 3 AM every single morning just listening to the house settle and waiting for the sun to come up. But me? Oh, no. 

By the time evening rolls around, after all that puttering and organizing and volunteering I was telling you about, I am just plum tuckered out. I usually have my cup of decaf tea, maybe watch a little Jeopardy or Wheel of Fortune, and I am in bed by 10 o'clock sharp. And I sleep right through until about 6 or 6:30 in the morning. So that's a good eight solid hours, which I think is pretty normal for anyone, let alone someone my age. 

I really do need my full night's rest to keep up with myself the next day! If I didn't get my sleep, I don't know how I'd manage all the projects I end up starting. So, no, I definitely haven't noticed needing less sleep. Once my head hits that pillow, I am out like a light, just like I was twenty years ago. It’s really just the daytime where my engine is running high and I can’t seem to stop moving. But at night, oh yes, I absolutely need my full rest. I've always been a good sleeper, ever since I was a little girl, really.

turns.doctor_question: During these times when you’re constantly busy, do you feel unusually cheerful or high in spirits?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well, no... I wouldn't say unusually cheerful. I mean, I'm a fairly positive person, generally speaking, always have been. My mother used to say I was born with a smile on my face, but I certainly don't feel like I'm walking on air or anything like that. I'm just... normal cheerful, I suppose? Like, if the sun is shining or if I see a nice cardinal at the bird feeder out the kitchen window, I'll feel happy about it. But it's not like I'm bursting with joy for no reason while I'm cleaning out that front hall closet or organizing the church bake sale. 

In fact, sometimes when I'm so busy, I actually feel a little bit frustrated with myself! Like, I'll be scrubbing the baseboards in the guest room—and nobody has even stayed in the guest room since my nephew visited three years ago—and I'll think to myself, "Why on earth am I doing this right now? I should be resting." So it's definitely not a feeling of being high in spirits or overjoyed. It's more of a restless energy, like a motor running inside me that just won't shut off, rather than a feeling of being overly happy. 

I mean, sure, it feels nice to get things done, and I like checking things off a list, but it's not an unusual kind of happiness. I'm not running around singing show tunes or feeling like I won the lottery. I'm just... busy. Just constantly, constantly busy, and maybe a little tired of being so busy, if I'm being perfectly honest. I just wish I could sit down and enjoy a cup of tea without feeling like I need to go wipe down the counters while the water is boiling, you know? So, no, not unusually cheerful at all. Just my regular self, but with far too much energy for an 87-year-old woman!

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes experiencing a 'restless energy'.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient states she is 'constantly, constantly busy' and feels like she has 'a motor running inside me that just won't shut off'.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient explicitly denies feeling unusually cheerful, high in spirits, or overjoyed.

turns.doctor_question: Do you spend a lot of time worrying about everyday things?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, heavens no, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. I mean, everyone has their little concerns, don't they? Like, if there's a big storm coming, I might wonder if the sump pump in the basement is going to hold up, because back in '98—or was it '99?—we had that awful flooding and it was just a mess. But I don't sit around wringing my hands over it. I just go down and check the pump, and maybe move a few boxes off the floor just in case, and then I'm on to the next thing. 

I'm really not one of those people who sits in their chair fretting about the bills or what the neighbors think or if the roast is going to be dry for Sunday dinner. My friend Gladys, bless her heart, she worries about everything under the sun. She'll call me up and talk for an hour about whether she offended the mailman by not saying good morning quickly enough, and I just think, "Gladys, the mailman has already forgotten about it!" 

But me? No, I don't have the time to sit and worry! Like I said, I'm always up and doing something. If a thought about something everyday pops into my head, like, "Oh, did I remember to buy stamps?", I don't sit and stew about it. I just pop up right then and there, go check my desk drawer, and if I don't have stamps, well, I might just grab my purse and head to the post office right that minute, even if I was in the middle of folding laundry. I just do it. So, I don't really spend time *worrying*, no. I just take action, probably faster than I should sometimes! But no, I wouldn't call myself a worrier at all.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes being 'always up and doing something' and constantly taking immediate action rather than sitting still.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly and repeatedly denies being a worrier or spending time fretting about everyday things.

turns.doctor_question: During these energetic times, do you feel more important, unusually confident, or especially capable compared with your usual self?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I'm just me! I'm just Margaret. I don't feel like I'm suddenly the Queen of England or the CEO of some big company just because I have the energy to clean the gutters out. 

I know some people get like that, you know, they get a little burst of energy and suddenly they think they know everything about everything. Like my brother-in-law, Arthur, rest his soul. Whenever he'd get a new hobby, whether it was woodworking or investing in the stock market—which he knew absolutely nothing about, let me tell you—he'd talk to you like he was the world's foremost expert. He'd stand there at the Thanksgiving table, carving the turkey, and lecturing us all about mutual funds as if he'd invented them. It was exhausting, really. 

But I'm not like that. I don't feel any more important or capable than I did yesterday or the day before. I know exactly what I can and can't do. I know I'm an 87-year-old woman who shouldn't be climbing up on a stepstool to dust the top of the china cabinet, but sometimes I just can't help myself because my body just wants to move. But it's not because I feel invincible or unusually confident! I actually know it's a bit foolish while I'm doing it. I'll be up there thinking, "Margaret, if you fall and break a hip, your daughter is going to be furious," but the urge to just get it done is so strong. 

So, no, there's no grand feeling of importance. I don't feel like I could go run for mayor or solve all the world's problems. I just feel like I need to keep busy, keep my hands moving, keep doing things around the house. It's just my normal self, just... sped up, I suppose you could say. But definitely not feeling more important or anything grand like that. Just regular old me, with a motor that won't quit.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes herself as having 'a motor that won't quit' and says her 'body just wants to move'.

turns.doctor_question: Has there been a clear period when this restless, busy energy was a noticeable change from your usual self?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've always been a doer, as I said. Always on the go, always keeping a tidy house and making sure everything is just so. But... yes, I suppose there has been a change. A very distinct change, actually, if I really stop and think about it. 

It hasn't always been this... relentless. This feeling like I simply cannot sit still. I'd say it really started getting noticeably worse, where it felt like a real shift from my usual self, about a year and five months ago. I remember the timing quite well because it was right around the time all those awful insurance bills started piling up, and then, wouldn't you know it, the roof started leaking in the sunroom. It never rains but it pours, right? Literally, in the case of the sunroom! 

Anyway, dealing with the insurance people on the phone—which is a full-time job in itself, let me tell you, pressing one for this and two for that and waiting on hold for forty-five minutes just to speak to a person who doesn't even know what a sunroom is—and then trying to coordinate with the roofers... it was just so much. And to cope with it all, I started taking on more responsibilities down at the senior center. I thought, "Well, Margaret, if you're going to be stressed, you might as well be useful." 

So I started organizing the Tuesday morning bingo, and then I took over the hospitality committee, which means baking two dozen muffins every Thursday, and before I knew it, I was practically running the place. And ever since then, ever since that period about a year and five months ago, this restless energy just hasn't let up. It’s like I shifted into high gear to get through the roof and the bills and the bingo, and I just never found the brakes again. Even now that the roof is fixed—thank goodness, they did a wonderful job, though the shingles are a slightly different shade of gray than the old ones, but you can only tell in a certain light—I still feel like I'm running at top speed. So, yes, that would be the clear period when it really changed from just being an active person to being this... constantly humming motor.

turns.doctor_question: During this period, have you had to go to the hospital or gotten into serious trouble because of all this energy and activity?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. The hospital? Goodness, at my age, you try to stay as far away from the hospital as you possibly can, because you go in for a stubbed toe and you come out with pneumonia! So, no, nothing like that. And serious trouble? Well, I suppose the only trouble I get into is with my daughter. She’s always scolding me, saying, "Mom, you’re going to hurt yourself, you need to just sit down and watch television like a normal person." 

But I haven't done anything that required a doctor or the police, if that's what you mean! I mean, I did have a little mishap... oh, when was it? Last Tuesday, I think. Yes, Tuesday, because it was the day the garbage gets collected. I was rushing to get the bins out, and I realized I hadn't emptied the little wastebasket in the guest bathroom, so I was practically running through the hall with this trash bag, and I tripped over the cord of the vacuum cleaner—which I had left out because I was planning to do the rugs right after the trash. I took a bit of a tumble, I won't lie. Scraped my shin right on the leg of the hall table. 

But did I go to the hospital? Absolutely not. I just marched myself into the kitchen, got a bag of frozen peas—the petite peas, mind you, they mold to the leg much better than the regular ones—and sat with it for exactly ten minutes before I realized I still needed to get that bin out before the truck came. I didn't even tell my daughter about it because she would have made a huge fuss and tried to take my vacuum away or something ridiculous.

So, no, no serious trouble. Just a few bruises here and there from moving a bit too fast and bumping into the corners of the coffee table. But certainly nothing that would put me in the emergency room or get me into any real trouble. I'm energetic, yes, and maybe a bit too hasty for my own good sometimes, but I'm not reckless! I still have my wits about me, thank goodness.

turns.doctor_question: During these periods, do you find yourself talking much more than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Talking more than usual? Well, I suppose you might have to ask my daughter about that, because she always says I talk a mile a minute, but if you ask me, I'd have to say no. No, I don't think I'm talking any more than I usually do. I've just always been a conversationalist, you see. 

Ever since I was a little girl, my mother used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. But I really haven't noticed any change in how much I speak since this whole restless period began. I still have my regular weekly phone calls with my sister, Beatrice—she lives out in Scottsdale now, you know, she moved there for the dry air because of her arthritis, which she absolutely swears by, though honestly I couldn't stand the heat myself, baking in the sun like a lizard on a rock. Anyway, we talk for exactly one hour every Sunday afternoon, just like we always have. 

And down at the senior center, well, yes, I talk to people when I'm handing out the bingo cards or serving the muffins, but that's just being polite, isn't it? You can't just shove a blueberry muffin at someone and walk away in dead silence. You have to ask about their grandchildren, or how their hydrangeas are doing. Take Mrs. Higgins, for instance—she has the most beautiful hydrangeas, though she uses entirely too much coffee grounds in the soil if you ask me, which makes them a bit too acidic, but I digress. 

The point is, I'm just making normal conversation. I'm not suddenly babbling at people or cornering them in the grocery store aisle to talk their ear off about nothing. I might be moving faster, and I might be doing three things at once—like dusting the baseboards while I'm on the cordless phone with Beatrice—but the talking itself hasn't sped up or gotten out of hand. I'm certainly not talking to myself, thank goodness! Well, except to say, "Margaret, where on earth did you put your reading glasses," but everyone at my age does that. So, no, my talking is just the same as it's always been. I'm just a sociable person, but I haven't turned into a chatterbox just because I have all this extra energy.

turns.doctor_question: At any time in your life, have you ever had a period when you felt depressed nearly every day for at least two weeks?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, like I was saying, I really haven't. Not for two weeks, not every day, nothing like that. I just don't have it in me to be down in the dumps for that long. There's always something that needs doing! 

I mean, just think about it—if I were depressed for two whole weeks, the house would fall to pieces. Who would polish the silver? My daughter certainly wouldn't, she puts everything in the dishwasher, which just ruins the finish, absolutely ruins it. And the garden! The weeds don't care if you're feeling sad, they just keep growing. I remember one time, I think I had a bad cold, or maybe it was the flu—this was back in, oh, 1998 maybe? I had to stay in bed for three days, and when I finally got up, the dust on the mantelpiece was thick enough to write my name in. I couldn't stand it. 

So, no, I just don't let myself get that way. If I ever feel a little bit blue, I just find a project. I'll reorganize the pantry, or I'll go through the old photo albums and put them in chronological order—which is a huge task, let me tell you, because nobody ever wrote dates on the back of the pictures in the seventies. You have to guess based on how wide my husband's lapels were! But it keeps the mind busy, you see. You can't be depressed if your mind is busy and your hands are moving. turns.doctor_question: At any other time in your life, have you ever had a period when you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Lost interest in things? Oh, absolutely not. Good heavens, I have too many interests to keep up with as it is! If I lost interest in things, I honestly don't know what I'd do with myself all day. 

I mean, take my knitting, for example. I've been knitting since I was, oh, maybe eight years old? My grandmother taught me. She used to make these incredibly intricate cable-knit sweaters, the kind that weigh about ten pounds and keep you warm in a blizzard. I don't make those anymore, my hands get a bit stiff if I try anything too complicated, but I still knit baby blankets for the hospital. I must have made at least fifty of them this year alone. Yellow and mint green are my favorites to use, because you never know if it's going to be a boy or a girl, and I think those colors are just so cheerful. I haven't lost a bit of interest in that. I'm actually working on a lovely lemon-yellow one right now with a scalloped edge, which is a new pattern I found in a magazine at the dentist's office. 

And then there's my baking. Oh, I could never lose interest in baking! Just last week, I made three dozen snickerdoodles for the church bake sale. I always use a pinch of cream of tartar, that's the secret, you see, it makes them perfectly chewy in the middle. Some people just use baking powder, but it's not the same, it really isn't. And my garden, well, I already mentioned my garden, didn't I? The weeds certainly don't let you lose interest. 

So, no, I've never had a time where I didn't want to do the things I enjoy. If anything, my problem is that there aren't enough hours in the day to do everything I want to do! I'm always finding new little projects. Just yesterday I decided I was going to learn how to make my own preserves. I bought a flat of strawberries from the farmer's market—though they were terribly overpriced, if you ask me, four dollars for a little pint!—and I'm going to try canning them this afternoon. So you see, I'm just as interested in my hobbies as I've always been, maybe even more so lately with all this energy I have!

turns.doctor_question: Before this started a year and five months ago, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt this same kind of unusually restless, driven energy?
turns.patient_response:
Before a year and five months ago? Oh, heavens, yes! Goodness me, you make it sound like it just appeared out of thin air. No, no, if you ask anyone who has known me for any length of time, they will tell you I have always been a bit like a motor that simply won't switch off. 

I mean, going all the way back! I remember very clearly being in grade school—this would have been, oh, the early nineteen-forties, I suppose. We had those heavy wooden desks, you know the ones with the little inkwells built right into the top right corner? Well, I simply could not stay in mine to save my life. I was always getting scolded for popping out of my seat. I'd rush up to the chalkboard, or I'd run over to the window because I saw a robin, or I'd just stand up because my legs felt like they had springs in them and sitting felt almost painful. 

And the talking! Oh, my mother used to say I was vaccinated with a phonograph needle. I was constantly talking over my classmates, just blurting things out because I couldn't hold the thought in my head for another second. The teachers were always writing notes home or pulling me aside. I remember one teacher in particular, Mrs. Gable—she wore these terribly strict wool skirts—she told my parents that I was just 'too lively.' That was the exact phrase she used, 'too lively.' And this was long, long before I was a teenager! 

So this feeling, this restless sort of drive to keep moving and doing... oh, it's not new at all. It’s just how I’m built. Even when I was a young woman, before I met my husband, I would walk miles and miles every single day just to burn it off. I simply can't sit still for long, I never have been able to. I always have to be doing something with my hands or my feet, which I suppose is why I get so much knitting done, like I was telling you earlier.
